https://www.thetimes.com/article/beware-.title: Beware the wave of radical, activist OAPs
https://www.thetimes.com/article/beware-.text:
It sounds like the start of a laboured joke. What allegedly links the ex-head of MI6, an obscure Cambridge historian, a marquess, a major general and a publishing tycoon? Well, for one thing, their emails were stolen by a Russian hacking operation. Carefully parsed by journalists at Computer Weekly, those leaked emails reveal a misfiring conspiracy among the pro-Brexit British establishment.
Mobilised by Sir Richard Dearlove (MI6) and Gwythian Prins (Cambridge), the network’s schemes included “hiring ex-MI6 operatives to spy on ‘remainers’, [and] running a ‘mole’ in the civil service”. Only through dark political arts could Brexit be secured and the Chinese Communist Party be banished from Britain.
Dearlove and Prins’s influence campaign combined covert operations, public advocacy and private lobbying. Though the campaign’s leaders had access to senior Conservative ministers and sent regular briefings to No 10, they reportedly “struggled to translate their access to policymakers into influence”. The group just about managed to place op-eds in sympathetic newspapers.
The Russian hacking group who stole the messages claimed that they added up to a deep-state coup. But what they actually revealed, as Computer Weekly put it, was “more Dad’s Army” than deep state; more Mick Herron than Ian Fleming.
Everybody involved in this failed Banana Kingdom plot was a retired septuagenarian. What really linked these men, apart from their crankishly paranoid politics, was their advanced age. Increasingly in Britain, radical politics and retirees find each other the way sharks find blood.
Retirement used to be an invitation to the golf course or to volunteer at a National Trust property. Retirees “got by” on their state pension. They didn’t dare eat pasta, because like my late grandmother they believed it was somehow “foreign”. Radical politics was for the young. Every revolution in history started as the brainfart of twenty-something underemployed pamphleteers in cheap cafés.
No longer. The roles of old and young have reversed. Peel the skin off every radical political movement of the past decade and you will find age, not youth, flowing through its veins. In Scotland, where SNP members seriously believed Alex Salmond’s claims that £1.5 trillion of untapped oil and gas reserves would float the country into a glorious post-Union future, 40 per cent of the members were over the age of 60.
A few years later a poll showed that grassroots Tories (you can guess their age) would have happily sacrificed that Union for Brexit. Even Corbynism, which was supposedly charged by the electricity of a digital “youthquake”, was a revolt of the elderly: half of new party members during Corbyn’s spell as leader were over the age of 55.
Radical pensioners were the lifeblood of Extinction Rebellion. The movement was defined not by students but by pensioners with too much time on their hands. Just Stop Oil, ER’s successor, has the same greying foot-soldiers. Attending any trial of its members is revealing. You look at the defendants, activists who glued themselves to national highways, expecting to see students with nose piercings and instead see cardigan-wearing pensioners. JSO activists who’ve been processed by the courts include a 76-year-old grandmother who climbed on to an M25 gantry. Her co-defendants last year were aged 72, 65 and 56.
It would take a serious sociologist and a disregard for certain political niceties to work out why so many industries in Britain — publishing, academia, media, tech and finance come to mind — have made such big bets on diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) since the death of George Floyd in May 2020. One undervalued reason may be that the people making decisions in those industries are getting on a bit. A generation raised on Street Fighting Man and half-remembered student protests saw the social justice movements of the late 2010s as a last shot at making their ideals a reality.
Older people are becoming a larger proportion of the population. In 1990 the percentage of people over the age of 65 was about 16 per cent; today it is closer to 20 per cent. The Office for National Statistics is forecasting that 25 per cent of the population will be over 65 by 2050. We tend to view this silver wave as an unsettling problem for the NHS and social care services, or to moan about the wealth pensioners have stored up in their homes. But some of the most profound consequences will be political.
With time to kill and decades ahead of them, pensioners will be well placed to attend rallies, organise strikes and contrive plots. Splenetic pensioners pushed the Conservative Party rightwards after Brexit. Sir Keir Starmer’s remarkably under-reported “mission document” for the next government boasts of plans to devolve “decision-making away from Westminster to those with the experience, knowledge and expertise”.
Starmer and some of his senior advisers are known to be interested in using citizens’ assemblies to cut through knotty issues. I’m sure they imagine that these bodies will be progressive. The likelihood is that they will be stuffed with the kinds of activists who have made JSO such an appealing part of public life. Nobody in their thirties and forties is going to have time to sit around on citizens’ assemblies. They will be gerontocratic institutions, in a nation where the old are growing ever more radical. Be wary of giving them more power than they deserve.
Will Lloyd is a commissioning editor and writer at the New Statesman

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/home.title: Home Office hires hangar to practise forcing migrants on to Rwanda flights
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/home.subtitle: Revealed: Staff will be trained in various scenarios at a secret location as the government ‘intensifies’ preparations for the first removals
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/home.text:
The Home Office has hired an aircraft hangar and a fuselage to enable security officials to practise forcibly removing migrants on to planes in preparation for Rwanda deportation flights, The Times can reveal.
Migrants will be escorted from a detention facility on an airbase one by one by security guards. As part of preparations for the first flights, the guards have undergone special training programmes to deal with “disruptive” people.
Staff will mimic different scenarios that the Home Office expects them to encounter when they move migrants on to aircraft bound for Kigali.
Scenarios that are being practised include migrants resorting to violence to prevent being put on a plane or Extinction Rebellion-style protests where individuals “play dead” by lying on the floor and refusing to move. They are also preparing for the prospect of dirty protests and demonstrations by campaigners outside the airbase in an attempt to halt flights.
It is estimated that five officers will be needed for each migrant being removed.
Individuals being trained include immigration enforcement officers and overseas escorting staff from the private security firm Mitie, which has a multimillion-pound contract with the Home Office for managing asylum and immigration detention facilities.
All overseas escorts must undergo a training course known as the Home Office Manual for Escorting Safely alongside a wider specialist training programme that ensures escorts know how to safely remove people from the country.
On Thursday, Rishi Sunak said that the government was “intensifying” its preparations for the first Rwanda flights. However, The Times has been told that Home officials believe they will not be feasible until June.
Sources said that it will take between 8 and 12 weeks to make the Safety of Rwanda Bill operational after it becomes law, and the government is not expecting it to receive royal assent until the end of March.
Baroness Davidson of Lundin Links has criticised the focus on a policy which has split the Conservative party over other methods of controlling immigration.
She agreed that “every sovereign nation should be in charge of who comes in” but asked on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Friday: “Where is the balance in this, rather than some of the language that is being used, some of the knots that people are getting into?”
Davidson, a former Scottish Conservative leader and ally of Lord Cameron, the foreign secretary, said: “This thing about putting people on planes to Rwanda. I mean, there are dogs in the street that know that, one, it is probably never going to happen. And two, if it does, it is going to be a number so small that it makes very little difference to the bottom line.”
The location of the aircraft hangar, which is normally hired as a film studio by production companies, has not been disclosed but a government source said that the Home Office had signed a one-year contract for the site.
• Sketch: Rishi Sunak looks for a Rwanda scapegoat: enter the Lords
The department has confirmed the plans and said that they were vital in order to ensure escorts can respond “professionally to the challenges of removing people with no right to be in the UK”.
A spokesman added: “This includes practical sessions so escorts have the skills they need to deal with different scenarios. As we ramp up removal activity we will continue to ensure new escorts have the training facilities necessary.”
The first Rwanda flights are understood to be expected to take off from the Ministry of Defence airfield at Boscombe Down near Salisbury, Wiltshire. This is where the first deportation flight was due to leave for Kigali in June 2022 until the plane was grounded at the eleventh hour after the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg granted an interim injunction.
The Home Office requested the use of the airfield after Stansted pulled out at the last minute due to concerns over the bad publicity it would have generated for the airport and the risk of protests.
It is understood that the training has been carried out by Red Snapper, which offers specialist training services for law enforcement, crime prevention and offender management.
A government source said: “We have a very detailed operational plan to exercise and practice all manoeuvres that are needed to remove people because the logistics are huge. You have to marshal people and it’s such a big logistical challenge.
“You also have to pre-empt a situation where an individual may claim they were manhandled so you need proper space to remove people from their detained facility and have a highly detailed and organised boarding pattern.”
• The Times view on the Rwanda vote: The Lightweight Brigade
“They’ll be escorted one by one and that needs a lot of practice. Otherwise, you can end up in hot water.”
The plans have been revealed as the Home Office published new figures that showed the department has lost contact with 5,598 asylum seekers in the UK. They made up a third of the 17,316 cases that have been withdrawn in the last 12 months.
Fewer than a fifth of those whose claims have been withdrawn have left the UK. The remaining individuals have either been found or have resubmitted their asylum applications.
In a letter to the Commons home affairs committee, the Home Office also revealed that only 1.6 per cent of the 114,000 migrants who have arrived in small boats in the UK since 2018 have been removed from the country, a total of just 1,850.
The letter also disclosed that of the £120 million initial payment made to Rwanda last year, only 21 per cent has actually been spent on building facilities for migrants. The rest has been spent on schools, hospitals and job creation opportunities to help boost the Rwandan economy.
Separate figures revealed that 358 migrants crossed the Channel on Wednesday, the busiest day of small boat crossings so far this year. In total 614 migrants have crossed so far this year, more than four times the number that had arrived by this time last year.
Enver Solomon, chief executive of the Refugee Council, said: “The government’s plans will have devastating consequences for distressed and traumatised refugees from countries such as Afghanistan and Syria, who will be left in permanent limbo fending for themselves in the community with no formal status.
“The reality is that they will be in unsafe and dangerous situations as many of them will effectively disappear, facing the risk of abuse and exploitation to avoid waiting indefinitely to be shipped to Rwanda.
“It’s time for the government to admit that its draconian laws are not only unconscionable but entirely unworkable and will simply cause more human suffering.”

https://www.thetimes.com/article/fate-of.title: Fate of Grangemouth shows we’re way off-track
https://www.thetimes.com/article/fate-of.text:
The Tories want you to know that the world is getting more dangerous. First David Cameron, then Grant Shapps have popped up to flog the dead horse of their electoral prospects by warning of coming war and strife, as if we can’t see it with our own eyes.
Yet they are doing precious little to prepare Britain for this danger; in fact, quite the opposite. The government might be publishing documents waffling about the need for “resilience” but it is still pursuing policies that make us ever more dependent on others.
Last week there was a brief debate in the Commons on the closure of Grangemouth refinery, one of only six of its kind left in the UK. The owner, Petroineos, announced in November that the facility would stop refining oil and become an import terminal as early as next spring.
The plant supplies all of Scotland’s aviation fuel and most of its petrol. In the industry, it’s thought the closure will increase our need to import oil products by 16 per cent, as well as risking thousands of skilled jobs in the supply chain and cratering a whole region of Scotland’s economy. Yet the SNP MP for the constituency affected, Falkirk, did not even bother to show up to the debate and not a single Labour MP stood up to speak.
The government didn’t have much to say either about this terrible loss to our industrial capacity. The minister, Graham Stuart, was sanguine. It is “unlikely to drive up the price of petrol”, he said, because “prices are mainly driven by international markets”.
Well, yes, in a situation where Europe has decided to shutter swathes of its energy industry, we may well find that prices are increasingly driven by international events like, say, a crisis in the Red Sea. The question is why on earth are we pursuing such policies if, as Cameron warns, “We live in very unstable, uncertain and dangerous times.”
To be fair, if resilience can be measured in pages of policy documents, Britain is well on the way to success. The government published its “Critical imports and supply chains strategy” this week, four years in the making and comprising a muddled round-up of miscellanea related to trade, net zero and data collection.
The “strategy” has five parts, one of which is a general discussion of how to make it even easier for Britain to import more and more of its critical goods from abroad by signing trade deals, apparently unaware that the founding premise of the document is that free trade no longer provides sufficient security against external shocks.
Another section touts Britain’s supposedly successful “5G supply chain diversification”, begun in 2019, whose listed achievements fail to include any actual change in market share or even the removal of Huawei kit from our core telecoms network (still a work in progress), but instead consists of the launch of various “strategies”, “frameworks” and “coalitions”.
Far from providing any serious analysis of why the UK and its allies have lost competitiveness in critical industries, what risks this poses and how we might improve it, the paper is a compendium of underwhelming or failed half-measures — like the “semiconductor strategy”, the “net zero strategy”, the “powering up Britain strategy” and the “energy security strategy”, whose mere existence apparently stands in for any actual measure of success, such as productivity, prices or market share.
Meanwhile, the assets we do have, like North Sea oil and Grangemouth, which should be the basis for stabilising domestic energy supplies and building up potential new industries in offshore wind, energy storage or carbon capture, are being allowed to decline at precipitous pace.
It’s true the government has allowed through a few new North Sea projects after years of dithering, but the damage had already been done by windfall taxes and botched climate policy. Now, for every mention of the term “green jobs”, which don’t yet exist, a skilled worker, engineer or apprentice in an industry that does exist is laid off or driven abroad by premature closures, reckless new schemes and ludicrous official forecasts of our actual energy needs.
Refiners, for example, have been told for years that their products aren’t going to be needed because of the miracle of electric cars (all made in China). They have been hammered with a new emissions trading scheme, whose carbon price outstripped Europe’s for much of the past two years; mysteriously excluded from the planned new carbon border tax; and hit by protests like the gluing of climate activists to the roofs of Grangemouth facilities over the summer — all while being subject to voracious competition in the Middle East and Asia. In such an atmosphere, one can see why it might be hard to justify the large investments needed to update technology and fix technical problems in the UK.
In July, when I visited Grangemouth, Just Stop Oil had just been cleared out and locals described protesters’ demands for a closure of the refinery as a “catastrophic” and “devastating” prospect. Ultimately, however, it wasn’t Just Stop Oil that delivered the blow, but the ignorant suits in Whitehall.
Ten years ago, civil servants told energy companies we wouldn’t need long-term gas contracts or storage, so they began winding them up. The result was the gas crisis of 2021-22. Undeterred, they are now telling refineries we won’t need petrol, oil producers that we won’t need oil, and car companies that we won’t need the combustion engine. The result is mass disinvestment, a huge loss of skills and a perilous growing dependence on non-existent technologies and foreign suppliers. And MPs can’t even be bothered to show up and debate it all.
According to the government’s own supply chain data, nearly a fifth of all Britain’s critical imports pass through the Suez canal. That includes a sixth of all the oil products we consume, a number sure to grow as a result of Grangemouth’s closure. A switch to electric vehicles will increase rather than reduce that dependency, thanks to China’s domination of battery production. Such trade flows can’t simply be taken for granted. Indeed, without American might, they can’t even be defended.
Despite this our government continues to talk as if net zero, free trade and economic security are all wonderfully self-reinforcing ideas. Britain obviously cannot address its vulnerabilities by resorting to autarky, but we can address our excessive reliance on hostile suppliers or fragile trade routes and halt the self-harming domestic policies making it worse.
The answer is not to ramp up the rhetoric and increase our output of “strategy” documents. What’s needed is a broad initiative in the free world to regain competitiveness. If we were to do that, we wouldn’t need to trumpet our success with “diversification dashboards” and “security frameworks”. The trade flows would speak for themselves.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/ed-dave.title: Post Office scandal: Victims say Ed Davey ‘has questions to answer’
https://www.thetimes.com/article/ed-dave.subtitle: Tory minister calls on Lib Dem leader to ‘be honest with people’ over his role in Horizon IT fiasco
https://www.thetimes.com/article/ed-dave.text:
Sir Ed Davey has an obligation to “be honest with people” about his role in the Post Office scandal, a Conservative minister has said.
The Liberal Democrat leader is facing intense scrutiny for his response to the fiasco when he was postal affairs minister between 2010 and 2012. Davey has been accused of “fobbing off” victims after being made aware of concerns with the faulty Horizon software that led to hundreds of postmasters being wrongly convicted of theft, fraud and false accounting. Many were bankrupted or jailed and at least four people took their own lives.
Bim Afolami, economic secretary to the Treasury, said that Davey had a duty to explain why he did not “ask the right questions” at the time, but stopped short of joining calls for him to resign.
He told Today on BBC Radio 4: “To be honest, I’m not one who goes around saying that [someone] needs to resign, but I do think he needs to … be honest with people and explain why, as a minister, he didn’t ask the right questions.
“In my job, you get a huge amount of information, there are a lot of people in the civil service who are working very hard on your behalf, but what you have to do is you have to ask the key questions and interrogate what you’re told. And I think that Sir Ed needs to explain what he was told why he allowed certain things to develop in the way that they did.”
• Pressure grows to exonerate hundreds of victims• Post Office scandal: follow latest news and updates
On Sunday Rishi Sunak confirmed that the government was considering ways to exonerate those convicted. Only a fifth of those prosecuted lodged appeals.
Victims of the Post Office scandal have said that Davey has “serious questions to answer” and should consider his position over his role in the fiasco.
Since becoming Lib Dem leader, Davey has made regular calls for public figures to resign from important positions and has made 31 such demands on his Twitter/X account since April 2019. He was told by one postmistress to “look in the mirror”.
Jo Hamilton, the lead appellant in a landmark 2021 Court of Appeal hearing, told The Times that Davey should have “done his job”, adding: “Of course Davey should have been asking more questions. He’s the minister. What does he get his ministerial salary for if he’s not asking questions. What did he think, we were just moaning? I can’t believe it.
“If you’re the minister you deal with stuff — that is the job. You have to earn your money for doing the job like the rest of us. They’re called public servants but they do anything but serve the public.
“He always calls for other people’s resignations, now it’s time for him to look in the mirror.”
Of those who inspired Davey’s ire, some like Boris Johnson, then prime minister, Cressida Dick, the former Metropolitan Police commissioner, Matt Hancock, as health secretary and Richard Sharp, the BBC chairman, did eventually fall on their swords.
Other targets ranged from individual public servants to entire groups such as every Conservative MP and the board of Thames Water.
Postmistress Seema Misra, who was jailed while pregnant in November 2010, during Davey’s tenure as postal affairs minister, said that Davey should quit.
She said: “He was in a position of power, and he could have stepped forward to find out what was going on. He could have turned the whole thing around, but he chose not to. He’s definitely liable.”
Davey has recently expressed regret for “not doing more”, after it emerged that in 2010 he told Alan Bates, the leader of the campaign to get justice for those affected, that a meeting would not “serve any useful purpose”.
He has insisted he was lied to by the Post Office, which assured him there were no errors with the IT system and instead pursued 600 postmasters through the courts — forcing them to pay back cash they did not owe.
Liam Fox, the former defence secretary, urged Davey to “explain in the House of Commons the decisions he took at the time, or the decisions he didn’t take at the time”.
Fox said Davey should have been more inquisitive about why there was suddenly “a big outbreak of criminality”.
Joanna Cherry, an SNP MP who is also a KC, said those who served in government must accept some responsibility. She said while Lib Dems were “in the frame for fobbing off the victims of Post Office miscarriages of justice”, the Conservatives as those in power since 2010 “shouldn’t be off the hook” either.
Anger came from Karl Turner, a Labour MP who defended postmasters as a barrister. He said: “My criticism of Ed Davey is that he probably didn’t ask the right questions, or enough of them, but this was a sophisticated scam by certain officials at the Post Office, and they went to all lengths to avoid the truth coming out.”
• Meet the real Alan Bates who took on the Post Office and won
Davey “completely understands the victims’ anger at this appalling miscarriage of justice”, a Liberal Democrat spokesman said, adding that “in hindsight he wishes he could have done more to help them”, and that he was focused on getting justice and compensation to all those affected as quickly as possible.
“Ed deeply regrets not realising that the Post Office was lying to him and other ministers on an industrial scale in what amounts to a conspiracy against the public,” the spokesman continued.
“He will fully co-operate with the inquiry and is keen to give his evidence as soon as possible to help get to the bottom of this scandal.”
Davey was defended by Tim Farron, one of his predecessors as Lib Dem leader, who accused political opponents in the Conservative Party of “weaponising this tragedy to distract from their failure to get compensation to the victims quickly”.
Ministers of all parties have been misled by the Post Office, Farron argued. He said that Ed Davey became the first minister on the record to meet with Bates in October 2010 – seven years and five ministers after Bates’ first attempt.
The 19 demands he made and the reasons he gave for making them:
• Boris Johnson
As backbench MP and prime minister — A total of 16 calls, sometimes twice a day, for Johnson to go, usually for lying.
• Chris Grayling
As transport secretary — For the cost of bungled “no deal” Brexit ferry contracts
• Mark Field
As foreign office minister — For manhandling a female Greenpeace activist
• Dominic Cummings
As chief adviser to Boris Johnson — For allegedly breaking lockdown rules
• Robert Jenrick
As communities secretary — For approving a Conservative donor’s planning request
• Alok Sharma
As COP26 president — For being part of a Government which was planning a coal mine in Cumbria
• Cressida Dick
As Metropolitan Police commissioner — For disgraceful policing of the Sarah Everard vigil
• Matt Hancock
As health secretary — For being terrible at his job and utterly failing on PPE, care and test-and-trace but not because of his private life
• Rishi Sunak
As chancellor — First over fraudulent Covid business loans and then for his tax arrangements
• Priti Patel
As home secretary — For failing to help refugees from Ukraine
• Every Conservative MP
As Boris Johnson’s parliamentary majority — Davey said they should resign the whip and sit as independents rather than prop up the failing prime minister
• Kwasi Kwarteng
As chancellor — twice urged to quit, first for his rotten budget then for playing fairytale economics
• Richard Sharp
As BBC chairman — For failing to uphold British values and withstand Conservative attacks
• Thames Water board
As directors — For being a slow-moving car crash on financial and regulatory matters and destroying local environments

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/step.title: Stephen Fry urges King’s Guard to ditch bearskins made of real fur
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/step.subtitle: The actor has narrated a Peta video showing bears being hunted in Canada
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/step.text:
The King’s Guard is bringing “dishonour” to Britain by continuing to wear bearskin caps made of real fur, the actor and environmental campaigner Stephen Fry has said.
Made from the pelts of Canadian black bears, which the Ministry of Defence says have been killed in “legal and licensed hunting”, the tall caps are worn by the British Foot Guards, among whom are the King’s Guard that protect Buckingham Palace and St James’s Palace.
Fry, 66, the actor and former host of QI, supports a new campaign from the animal rights group Peta to replace fur with synthetic material. He has narrated a Peta video showing black bears in Canada being shot or killed with a crossbow before being dismembered.
It takes the skin of at least one bear to make a single Foot Guard cap. Peta argues that the MoD is incentivising bear hunting.
“Britain has always prided itself on being ‘sporting’, but these bears — lured with cookies to the hunters’ hiding place — stand no chance of survival,” Fry says in the video.
“Tradition is never an excuse for cruelty, which is why I’m joining the call for the Ministry of Defence to stop using the fur of slaughtered wildlife and make the switch to humane faux fur for the King’s Guard’s caps. To do otherwise would be unconscionable — and un-British.
“Every day that our soldiers wear hats from the fur of slaughtered bears brings dishonour to our country,” he adds. “It’s time for a changing of the guard.”
Fry has campaigned on the environment for some time, producing nature documentaries for ITV and calling on the public to support Extinction Rebellion. He is also a royalist and attended the King’s coronation in May, which he said was “enchanting and extraordinary”.
Bearskin caps were formally introduced after the Battle of Waterloo in 1815 to make soldiers taller and more intimidating. Now they are mostly preserved for soldiers taking part in ceremonial occasions such as Trooping the Colour. Each hat costs about £650 per pelt and they are meant to last decades, but the MoD orders about 100 a year.
Peta has designed a synthetic version, but the MoD has said various alternatives fail standards on water absorption, drying speed and compression. Peta tried and failed to stop the use of bearskin in the courts in 2022.
“The UK government is sponsoring bait-and-kill sport hunting of bears,” Kate Werner, a senior campaign manager at Peta, said. “It’s time to modernise this iconic symbol of Britain by switching to a fabulous faux fur that has been tested specifically to ensure its suitability for use by the King’s Guard.”
An MoD spokesperson said that its bear pelts were sourced from authorised hunts and a regulated Canadian fur market: “To date and to the department’s knowledge, an alternative has yet to meet the standards required to provide an effective replacement for the bearskin ceremonial caps.”

https://www.thetimes.com/world/article/m.title: Protesters throw soup at Mona Lisa in Paris
https://www.thetimes.com/world/article/m.subtitle: Our farmers are dying at work, say food activists at Louvre as they attack Da Vinci’s work, which is protected by a bulletproof screen
https://www.thetimes.com/world/article/m.text:
Protesters have splashed soup over the bulletproof glass protecting the Mona Lisa at the Louvre in Paris.
Video footage of the attack on Sunday morning showed two women, identified only as Sasha, 24, and Marie-Juliette, 63, hurling orange liquid at the painting by Leonardo Da Vinci.
They wore T-shirts bearing the French slogan Riposte Alimentaire (Food Response), the name of a group calling for sustainable agriculture to help tackle the climate crisis.
“What is more important? Art or the right to healthy and sustainable food?” the activists said. “Your agricultural system is sick. Our farmers are dying at work.”
The incident coincides with widespread protests by French farmers, who have blocked roads across the country in anger at falling prices, rising costs, environmental measures and a perceived lack of support from the government.
In a statement posted on X/Twitter, the group expressed concern for the farmers struggling to make a living while the food industry makes “excessive profits”. It added: “Farmers are squeezed by the pressures of mass distribution, going so far as to make them sell at a loss.”
The group, linked to the A22 Network of environmental protest organisations that includes Just Stop Oil in the UK, called on the French government to honour its climate commitments and establish a social security system that would introduce a monthly €150 food card for residents to buy “approved” products.
Environmental activists have repeatedly targeted well-known artworks around the world in an attempt to highlight their concerns. Paintings by Van Gogh, Klimt and Monet have been splattered with a range of substances including pea soup and mashed potatoes.
Staff were seen putting up black barriers between them and members of the public visiting the museum. The Mona Lisa, known in France as La Joconde and often described as the most famous painting in the world, is unlikely to have suffered any damage due to the protective screen.
A waist-height wooden railing has also been installed to try to prevent visitors getting too close, although in this case the activists simply ducked under the barrier.
The painting has been targeted several times in recent years. In May 2022 a man disguised as an elderly woman in a wheelchair threw custard pies at it.
After smearing white cream across the glass, the activist shouted “Think of the Earth” as he was led away by security staff. The 36-year-old man was sent to a police psychiatric unit.
A glass casing was first installed to protect the Mona Lisa in 1956 after it was doused with acid and smashed with a rock in two separate attacks.
The glass was also sprayed with paint in 1974 and hit with a ceramic mug in 2009.

https://www.thetimes.com/comment/registe.title: Corrections and clarifications 2021
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/registe.text:
Complaints about inaccuracies in all sections of The Sunday Times should be addressed to complaints@sunday-times.co.uk or Complaints, The Sunday Times, 1 London Bridge Street, London SE1 9GF. Find more details on our complaints procedure here. In addition, the Independent Press Standards Organisation (Ipso) will examine formal complaints about the editorial content of UK newspapers and magazines.
■ December 26, 2021
The Metropolitan Police have asked us to make clear that, contrary to the headline “It’s your job to stop men attacking women, Crown actress tells police” (News, December 12), Claire Foy said it was the responsibility of all men to challenge violence towards women.
We said the footwear chain Schuh had learned it will be dumped by Nike (Business, last week). Schuh denies this and says Nike has not discontinued supplying it and it will continue to have access to Nike products.
■ December 19, 2021
We said the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) had routinely missed chances to investigate cases properly (News, October 24). The CCRC disagrees with this and states that in the past decade only 18 CCRC cases out of the 291 that have been referred for appeal were initially rejected by the CCRC; and ten of those 18 cases related to a single CCRC review. We are happy to put this on record.
■ December 12, 2021
We wrongly said that the Republic of Ireland will require visitors from Northern Ireland to have a negative Covid test before entering the country (News, last week). Northern Ireland is exempt from the restrictions.
The 2017-19 examination results from Saint Martin’s School were mistakenly attributed to Solihull Senior School (Parent Power, last week). Saint Martin’s and Solihull School merged in 2020. We apologise for the error.
■ November 21, 2021
An interview with Lord Botham wrongly named the former chairman of Yorkshire county cricket club as Richard Hutton (Sport, last week). It should have referred to Roger Hutton. We apologise for any confusion caused.
■ November 14, 2021
A collection of Fabergé items to be sold by Christie’s belonged to the late Harry Woolf, founder of the Underwoods chain of chemists, not Lord Woolf, the former lord chief justice, as we wrongly stated (News in Brief, last week). We apologise for the error.
■ October 31, 2021
We wrongly said that a £1 Premium Bond has a one in 34,500 chance of winning a £1 million prize in the monthly draw (Money, October 10). In fact that is the probability of winning a £25 prize.
A winning entry in the Landscape Photographer of the Year awards (Magazine, last week) showed Kilchurn Castle, not Dunnottar Castle as the caption stated.
■ September 19, 2021
We said that Keir Starmer had written a 14,000-word mission statement with the help of Paul Ovenden and Philip Collins (News, last week). Philip Collins states that this was not the case and that he did not help to write the statement. We are happy to put this on record.
■ September 5, 2021
Our graphic “Taliban’s new arsenal” (News, last week) showed equipment supplied by the US to Afghan armed forces since 2001. How much of it is now in Taliban hands is not known. We regret any confusion caused.
■ August 22, 2021
The interview with Mary Trump in the Magazine last week incorrectly stated that her mother had died in 2001. In fact Linda Lea Clapp is alive and well. We apologise for the error.
■ August 15, 2021
Further to our article “Animals are sentient? Of course farmers want such a notion sent for slaughter” (Comment, August 1) the National Farmers Union has asked us to point out that it is broadly supportive of the Animal Welfare (Sentience) Bill. We are happy to do so.
Our article on incidents at Wimbish School in Essex (News, June 27) referred to a pupil being expelled. We have been informed that the expulsion was subsequently quashed by an independent review panel. We are happy to make this clear.
Our article “Race hate crimes on the rise in Scotland” (News, last week) stated that 4,687 cases of racially aggravated harassment or conduct crimes were recorded in Scotland in 2020-21, an increase of 6 per cent on the previous year. In fact, the number of cases was 1,782, a rise of 2 per cent. We apologise for the error.
A report on motorcycle safety (News, last week) wrongly referred to Cal Phillips as the daughter of Yvonne Motherwell. Cal Phillips is her son. We apologise for the error and the distress it caused.
■ August 1, 2021
Scotland’s Land Reform Act granted public access to Scottish lochs but it did not allow fishing without permission from the rights holder, contrary to the impression given in our article on the North Coast 500 (Travel, last week).
■ July 25, 2021
A recent offer to buy the supermarket chain Morrisons was worth £6.3 billion, rather than £6.3 million as we wrongly stated (Business, last week).
■ July 4, 2021
Our column “The culture war is a conflict no one meant to start” (Comment, last week) incorrectly described Cecil Rhodes as a slave-owner. Slavery had been abolished in the British Empire before Rhodes was born. We apologise for the error.
Our article “The e-money ‘banks’ that charge 99p when you pay by card” (Money, last week) wrongly stated that MoneyMona is the trading name of Contis Financial Services. The two companies are entirely separate. Contis is a card issuer and payment processor that does not set fees for card users. We apologise for the error.
Our article “Gender clinic ‘converting’ gay children” (News, June 20) stated that a High Court judgment in 2020 banned the use of puberty-blocking drugs. The judgment in fact said it was unlikely that children under 16 could give informed consent to their use, and the NHS responded by halting referrals for such drugs. We are happy to make this clear.
■ June 6, 2021
Contrary to the implication of an article in Best Places to Live (March 28), Broughty Ferry is on the same side of the Tay estuary as Dundee. We apologise for the confusion.
■ May 16, 2021
We stated that Extinction Rebellion demands that the government make illegal all carbon emissions by 2025 (Comment, March 28). We have been asked to point out that the group’s demand is for the government to act now to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to net zero by 2025. We are happy to make this clear.
■ April 25, 2021
Our story “Forced to mourn alone, the Queen bids Philip goodbye” (News, last week) made reference to an offensive remark made by the Duke of Edinburgh during a visit to China. We did not intend to condone the remark. We apologise for the offence caused.
In “Heywood nominated Greensill for CBE” (News, April 4) we reported incorrectly that Jeremy Heywood, the former cabinet secretary, had worked for Morgan Stanley for five years before returning to the civil service in 2008. He was in fact there for three-and-a-half years, returning in 2007. We apologise for the error.
Contrary to the impression given in our article “David Cameron rode the wave of Covid to target the NHS” (News, last week), Sir David Dalton was not a member of the Advisory Board of Earnd. His role as a paid advisor to the company started in June 2020, three months after he gave an interview which expressed support for salary demand scheme technology generally, without specifying any provider. Sir David states that there was no connection between this interview and his appointment. We are happy to make this clear.
■ March 28, 2021
Lord Palmer has asked us to point out that his family sold its interest in the company Huntley & Palmers to Nabisco, not to RJ Reynolds Tobacco (News, last week). RJ Reynolds acquired Nabisco the following year. He has also asked us to point out that Huntley & Palmers was founded by his great-great-uncle, not his great-grandfather. We apologise for the errors.
■ March 21, 2021
Recent surveys show that 15 per cent of Poles never attend church, not 50 per cent as we wrongly stated (World News, last week).
■ March 7, 2021
The “letter of assurance” against prosecution received by the IRA member John Downey was not part of the Good Friday agreement, as we wrongly stated (News Review, last week). Such letters were provided by the UK government after the agreement was signed.
■ February 28, 2021
The new lay member of the House of Commons committee on standards will not be considering claims of bullying and harassment, as we wrongly claimed (Atticus, Comment, February 21). Such cases will be dealt with by a separate body, the Independent Expert Panel.
We said that no members of the Scotland rugby team took the knee before their international against England earlier this month (Sport, February 14). In fact, four players did so.
■ February 14, 2021
Following our report “Battle looms as Oxford prepares to topple Rhodes” (News, last week), Oxford University has asked us to make clear that the decision on whether to remove a statue of Cecil Rhodes will be made by Oriel College rather than the university itself. We are happy to do so.
The same article wrongly stated that a Benin Bronze statue of a cockerel is to be returned to Nigeria by St John’s College, Cambridge. In fact the statue will be returned by Jesus College.
The article also stated that Rhodes made money through a company that used slave labour. We have been asked to make clear that the term “slave labour” was intended to describe the oppressive and degrading conditions for workers who were paid for their labour.
The Mauritanian is wrongly attributed as a Netflix film in today’s Magazine. We apologise for the error.
■ January 17, 2021
The item “Dance your way out of this row, folks” (Rod Liddle, Comment, September 13), which mistakenly stated that no opinion polls were available on the level of popular support for the Black Lives Matter movement, was also wrong to imply that information was being withheld from the public. We have been asked to point out that the polls that were conducted found a wide range of views, not supporting the writer’s suspicion that the mass of the public finds the movement repellent. We are happy to make this clear.
Our report “KPMG hired to unearth Russian gold miner Petropavlovsk’s ‘dodgy deals’” (Business, November 22) said that Jay Hambro was “running” IRC Limited. Mr Hambro does not run IRC Limited, having resigned as Executive Chairman and Chief Investment Officer in January 2016, and he was not running the company during the period covered by Petropavlovsk PLC’s investigation. We are happy to make this clear.
■ January 4, 2021
David Walsh’s column on doping in horse racing (Sport, December 27) mistakenly used a photograph showing the filly Anapurna with Mark Weinfeld of The Meon Valley Stud. Mr Weinfeld, the stud and the filly have never been associated with doping, and no such implication was intended. We apologise for the distress caused.
■ January 3, 2021
Our article “Mitie merger maestro ousted” (Business, November 29) wrongly stated that Karen Thomas-Bland had been dismissed from her role as Mitie’s programme integration director after the chief executive, Phil Bentley, lost faith in her performance. The decision to leave Mitie was Ms Thomas-Bland’s own. She resigned her position amicably as she had completed her work on this project. The company has said in a statement that “she has decided to focus on new challenges and … leaves with our thanks”, having “laid all the foundations for a successful integration”. We apologise to Ms Thomas-Bland for this error.

https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.title: Beware the wave of radical, activist OAPs
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.text:
It sounds like the start of a laboured joke. What allegedly links the ex-head of MI6, an obscure Cambridge historian, a marquess, a major general and a publishing tycoon? Well, for one thing, their emails were stolen by a Russian hacking operation. Carefully parsed by journalists at Computer Weekly, those leaked emails reveal a misfiring conspiracy among the pro-Brexit British establishment.
Mobilised by Sir Richard Dearlove (MI6) and Gwythian Prins (Cambridge), the network’s schemes included “hiring ex-MI6 operatives to spy on ‘remainers’, [and] running a ‘mole’ in the civil service”. Only through dark political arts could Brexit be secured and the Chinese Communist Party be banished from Britain.
Dearlove and Prins’s influence campaign combined covert operations, public advocacy and private lobbying. Though the campaign’s leaders had access to senior Conservative ministers and sent regular briefings to No 10, they reportedly “struggled to translate their access to policymakers into influence”. The group just about managed to place op-eds in sympathetic newspapers.
The Russian hacking group who stole the messages claimed that they added up to a deep-state coup. But what they actually revealed, as Computer Weekly put it, was “more Dad’s Army” than deep state; more Mick Herron than Ian Fleming.
Everybody involved in this failed Banana Kingdom plot was a retired septuagenarian. What really linked these men, apart from their crankishly paranoid politics, was their advanced age. Increasingly in Britain, radical politics and retirees find each other the way sharks find blood.
Retirement used to be an invitation to the golf course or to volunteer at a National Trust property. Retirees “got by” on their state pension. They didn’t dare eat pasta, because like my late grandmother they believed it was somehow “foreign”. Radical politics was for the young. Every revolution in history started as the brainfart of twenty-something underemployed pamphleteers in cheap cafés.
No longer. The roles of old and young have reversed. Peel the skin off every radical political movement of the past decade and you will find age, not youth, flowing through its veins. In Scotland, where SNP members seriously believed Alex Salmond’s claims that £1.5 trillion of untapped oil and gas reserves would float the country into a glorious post-Union future, 40 per cent of the members were over the age of 60.
A few years later a poll showed that grassroots Tories (you can guess their age) would have happily sacrificed that Union for Brexit. Even Corbynism, which was supposedly charged by the electricity of a digital “youthquake”, was a revolt of the elderly: half of new party members during Corbyn’s spell as leader were over the age of 55.
Radical pensioners were the lifeblood of Extinction Rebellion. The movement was defined not by students but by pensioners with too much time on their hands. Just Stop Oil, ER’s successor, has the same greying foot-soldiers. Attending any trial of its members is revealing. You look at the defendants, activists who glued themselves to national highways, expecting to see students with nose piercings and instead see cardigan-wearing pensioners. JSO activists who’ve been processed by the courts include a 76-year-old grandmother who climbed on to an M25 gantry. Her co-defendants last year were aged 72, 65 and 56.
It would take a serious sociologist and a disregard for certain political niceties to work out why so many industries in Britain — publishing, academia, media, tech and finance come to mind — have made such big bets on diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) since the death of George Floyd in May 2020. One undervalued reason may be that the people making decisions in those industries are getting on a bit. A generation raised on Street Fighting Man and half-remembered student protests saw the social justice movements of the late 2010s as a last shot at making their ideals a reality.
Older people are becoming a larger proportion of the population. In 1990 the percentage of people over the age of 65 was about 16 per cent; today it is closer to 20 per cent. The Office for National Statistics is forecasting that 25 per cent of the population will be over 65 by 2050. We tend to view this silver wave as an unsettling problem for the NHS and social care services, or to moan about the wealth pensioners have stored up in their homes. But some of the most profound consequences will be political.
With time to kill and decades ahead of them, pensioners will be well placed to attend rallies, organise strikes and contrive plots. Splenetic pensioners pushed the Conservative Party rightwards after Brexit. Sir Keir Starmer’s remarkably under-reported “mission document” for the next government boasts of plans to devolve “decision-making away from Westminster to those with the experience, knowledge and expertise”.
Starmer and some of his senior advisers are known to be interested in using citizens’ assemblies to cut through knotty issues. I’m sure they imagine that these bodies will be progressive. The likelihood is that they will be stuffed with the kinds of activists who have made JSO such an appealing part of public life. Nobody in their thirties and forties is going to have time to sit around on citizens’ assemblies. They will be gerontocratic institutions, in a nation where the old are growing ever more radical. Be wary of giving them more power than they deserve.
Will Lloyd is a commissioning editor and writer at the New Statesman
